nameStory: The Squash Lady Beetle gets its name from its favorite food — plants in the squash family like cucumbers, melons, and of course, squash! Unlike most lady beetles that help gardeners by eating aphids, this yellow troublemaker has developed a taste for the leaves of our beloved garden vegetables.
description: The Squash Lady Beetle is a yellow, dome-shaped beetle that looks like a sunny version of the classic red ladybug. Each wing cover (called an elytron) displays seven prominent black spots, while four smaller black spots dot the shield-like area behind its head. At about the size of a typical ladybug, this plant-eating beetle can be found munching holes in the leaves of squash, cucumber, and melon plants throughout the eastern United States.

idTips.label: Yellow color with black spots
idTips.description: Bright yellow to orange-yellow body with contrasting black spots — much brighter than the pale yellow of cucumber beetles and lacking the red of beneficial ladybugs

idTips.label: Seven spots per wing cover
idTips.description: Each wing cover has exactly seven large, round black spots arranged in a distinctive pattern — count carefully as this is a key identifying feature

idTips.label: Four spots on thorax shield
idTips.description: The pronotum (the shield-like area behind the head) bears four small black spots, creating a total spot count that helps distinguish it from other spotted beetles

idTips.label: Dome-shaped body
idTips.description: Classic ladybug shape with a smooth, rounded dome that feels hard to the touch — not elongated like cucumber beetles

idTips.label: Found on cucurbit plants
idTips.description: Almost always discovered on squash, cucumber, melon, or pumpkin plants where it chews irregular holes in leaves, often in small groups

idTips.label: Size and texture
idTips.description: About the size of your pinky nail with a glossy, smooth shell that makes a tiny clicking sound when disturbed

habitat: Look for Squash Lady Beetles in gardens, farms, and anywhere cucurbit plants grow throughout New England's lower elevations. They're particularly common in home vegetable gardens, community gardens, and agricultural areas with rich, well-drained soil. You'll rarely find them away from their host plants — if you see squash, cucumber, or melon plants, scan the leaves carefully.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots in late spring and begin searching for young cucumber family plants to feed on and lay eggs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible feeding on leaves, and spiny yellow larvae can be found on the undersides of damaged leaves.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding to build up energy reserves before seeking shelter for winter, often becoming more concentrated as plants begin to decline.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter hidden under leaf litter, mulch, or other garden debris near their summer feeding areas, remaining inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This is one of the few 'bad guy' ladybugs in North America — while most of their cousins are beloved garden helpers that devour plant-destroying aphids, Squash Lady Beetles are actually the garden pests themselves, capable of completely defoliating a cucumber plant in just a few days when present in large numbers!
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for beneficial ladybugs (which are typically red or orange) or cucumber beetles (which are more elongated and pale yellow-green). Remember: if it's bright yellow, dome-shaped like a classic ladybug, and sitting on your squash plants eating holes in the leaves, it's probably this troublemaker, not a garden helper!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'Lady Beetle,' this species breaks the general rule that ladybugs are beneficial garden insects. It belongs to a small group of plant-eating lady beetles that have evolved away from the typical aphid-hunting lifestyle of their relatives, causing confusion for gardeners who expect all ladybugs to be helpful.
compareHints: The Squash Lady Beetle can be distinguished from its close relative, the Mexican Bean Beetle, by its host plant preference and slightly different spot pattern. While Mexican Bean Beetles prefer bean and lima bean plants, Squash Lady Beetles stick to cucumbers, squash, and melons. Both are yellow with black spots, but the Squash Lady Beetle's seven spots per wing cover and four thorax spots create a more consistent pattern than the somewhat variable spotting of its bean-loving cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mexican bean beetles are easily distinguished from their closest New England relative, the Squash Lady Beetle, by their host plants and habitat - squash beetles stick to cucurbits like squash and pumpkins, while Mexican bean beetles are found exclusively on legumes.
